summary: This informational memo describes how sites connect to multiple providers with IPv4, which is essential for many Internet sites. It lists features useful for comparing with multihoming proposals, especially those related to IPv6.

eli5.summary: Some sites use more than one internet provider so one failure does not cut them off. This document describes how that is done with the old addresses.

questions: how do sites connect to multiple isps
subtitle: How sites hook up to more than one provider with IPv4, and what each approach costs.

tldr.problem: Many Internet sites want to stay online if one provider fails, but IPv4 and CIDR were built around a hierarchy where each site hangs off one provider.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes three practices: multihoming with BGP (using provider-independent or provider-aggregatable addresses), multiple attachments to one transit provider, and NAT- or RFC 2260-based multihoming. It then compares them on 14 features such as redundancy, load sharing and scalability.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational snapshot of current practice, written so other multihoming proposals (particularly for IPv6) can be compared against it.

today: RFC 4116 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes IPv4 multihoming practice as of July 2005 and makes no security analysis of multihoming.

sections.title: Why Multihoming Matters
sections.content:
Multihoming means connecting a site to more than one transit provider. The RFC says it is an important component of service for many Internet sites and is widely used in the IPv4 Internet.

Current IPv4 multihoming practices were added on to the Classless Inter Domain Routing (CIDR) architecture (RFC 1519), which assumes routing table entries can be aggregated along a hierarchy of customers and service providers. The document records common practices and lists their features so they can be compared with other approaches.
sections.eli5: Imagine a house with two roads leading to it. If one road is closed you can still get out. Multihoming gives a network that kind of second road.

sections.title: Key Terms
sections.content:
A site is an entity that runs its own network using IP and decides its own addressing plan and routing policy. A transit provider gives a site connectivity to the wider Internet. A site is multihomed if it has more than one transit provider, and multi-attached if it has more than one layer-3 connection to a single provider.

Addresses come in two kinds. Provider-Independent (PI) addresses are globally unique and usually come from a Regional Internet Registry, not from a provider. Provider-Aggregatable (PA) addresses are assigned by a transit provider, so the routes for them are usually covered by that provider's aggregate route.
sections.eli5: PI addresses are like a phone number you own yourself. PA addresses are like a number your phone company lends you, so if you switch companies you must change it.

sections.title: Multihoming with BGP
sections.content:
The general approach is to announce a set of routes to two or more transit providers using BGP. The rest of the Internet then has multiple paths back to the site, and each provider is another possible path for outbound traffic.

PI addresses have long been the preferred approach, but RIR policies have tightened since the mid-1990s, when a /24 was the longest generally accepted prefix and was easy to get. Many small sites can no longer justify a PI block, and each PI site adds a prefix to the global routing system.

PA addresses let a site use space from one primary provider and have additional providers also announce its routes. Operators still commonly expect a minimum /24 prefix. Some networks filter long prefixes covered by a provider's aggregate, which increases reliance on the primary provider, and the site usually has to renumber if it leaves that provider.

On the AS number side, a site can use its own globally unique AS number, which gives a consistent origin and makes troubleshooting easier. It can instead use a private-use AS number, which is normally stripped from the AS_PATH, so routes look like they have inconsistent origins, or ask each provider to originate its routes.
sections.eli5: The site tells two different internet companies, "you can deliver mail to me." Then letters can come in through either one. The catch is that getting your own address block can be hard for small sites.

sections.title: Other Approaches: Multi-Attachment and NAT
sections.content:
A site can connect to a single transit provider in several places. This adds no load to the global routing table and does not require BGP, although some mechanism to reroute traffic after a failure is needed and BGP is often used. It gives no protection if the provider itself fails.

NAT- or RFC 2260-based multihoming uses PA addresses from each provider. Hosts get addresses per RFC 2260, or the site uses NAT to map the provider addresses to private-use addresses (RFC 1918). Providers need to do nothing special, no PI addresses or AS numbers are needed, and the global routing system carries no extra load. However, it does not address several common motivations, most notably transport-layer survivability.
sections.eli5: One way is to have two roads to the same town. Another is to keep two mailing addresses and pick whichever works. Neither is perfect.

sections.title: Comparing the Features
sections.content:
The comparison follows the goals in RFC 3582. All methods give some redundancy and some load sharing. BGP-speaking sites can use import and export policies to steer traffic, though the RFC says this is not comprehensive and many traffic engineering goals can only be loosely approximated.

For transport-layer survivability, BGP-based practices give some session survivability, but sessions may time out if convergence takes long. Sessions generally do not survive a re-homing event with RFC 2260/NAT multihoming. New sessions can be created after re-homing in every method.

On scalability, current practices are thought to contribute to significant growth of state in the global routing system (see RFC 3221). Only RFC 2260/NAT multihoming and multi-attaching add no state. Widespread use of methods needing AS numbers could also strain that finite resource.

The methods impose no new requirements on DNS or on hosts beyond those of singlehomed sites. Boundary routers may need BGP sessions with providers. Providers usually get authorisation before announcing a PA prefix of another provider, but no technical requirement or common contractual policy demands it.
sections.eli5: The authors grade each way on things like staying online, sharing the load and not cluttering the Internet's big address book. The BGP ways work best but add the most clutter.
